content: Cannabidiol, commonly referred to as CBD, is a non-intoxicating cannabinoid derived from the hemp plant, Cannabis sativa. It is one of the primary constituents of the plant, comprising up to 40% of its extracts. While CBD itself does not produce intoxicating effects, it appears to modulate the euphoric effects of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), which is an isomer of cannabidiol, and may impart a sedative quality. However, some studies suggest that CBD can enhance alertness. CBD may slow the clearance of THC from the body, potentially by interfering with its hepatic metabolism. Unlike THC, CBD does not seem to directly interact with the CB1 or CB2 cannabinoid receptors. From a medical perspective, CBD has demonstrated efficacy in alleviating convulsions, inflammation, anxiety, and nausea. Additionally, it has shown potential in inhibiting the proliferation of cancer cells. Recent research has indicated that CBD may be as effective as atypical antipsychotic medications in the treatment of schizophrenia. In April 2005, Canadian health authorities approved the use of Sativex, an oromucosal spray designed to alleviate pain associated with multiple sclerosis. Sativex contains both THC and CBD and is marketed in Canada by GW Pharmaceuticals. Furthermore, CBD has been shown to inhibit the growth of cancer cells while exhibiting low toxicity in non-cancerous cells. Although the precise mechanisms underlying this inhibitory effect are not yet fully understood, research by Ligresti et al. suggests that CBD exerts its effects through a combination of mechanisms. These include direct or indirect activation of CB2 and TRPV1 receptors, as well as the induction of oxidative stress, all of which contribute to the promotion of apoptosis in cancer cells.
